why: Coffee alertness starts within ~15-30 min, peaks around 1 h and fades over several hours (half-life ~5 h).
source: Smith 2002 Food Chem Toxicol; Nehlig 2010 J Alzheimers Dis; Fredholm 1999 Pharmacol Rev

why: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and lowers felt sleepiness for several hours after one coffee.
source: Drake 2013 J Clin Sleep Med; Landolt 2004; Fredholm 1999 Pharmacol Rev

why: Oral IR methylphenidate feels stimulating from ~30 min, peaks at 1-2 h and wears off in about 4 h.
source: Volkow 1998/2001 Am J Psychiatry (PET + VAS time course); Kollins 1998 Exp Clin Psychopharmacol; Swanson & Volkow 2003

why: Classroom and lab attention gains with IR methylphenidate last about 3-5 h, peaking 1-3 h after the dose.
source: Swanson 1998/2003 (laboratory classroom studies); Greenhill 2002 J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry

why: 10 mg oral dexamphetamine raises 'stimulated/vigor' ratings from ~30-60 min, peaking at 1.5-3 h and lasting 4-8 h.
source: de Wit 2002 Neuropsychopharmacology; Kirkpatrick 2012 Psychopharmacology; Asghar 2003 J Clin Psychopharmacol

why: Euphoria/'feel high' ratings after oral dexamphetamine peak around 1-3 h and decline before plasma levels do.
source: de Wit 2002; Angrist 1987; Kirkpatrick 2012 Psychopharmacology

why: Amphetamine suppresses appetite with a time course that follows its 1-3 h peak and lasts much of the day.
source: Silverstone 1983; Foltin 1990 Pharmacol Biochem Behav; Heal 2013 J Psychopharmacol

why: The meth 'high' comes within minutes when smoked (hours when oral), and fades faster than its long-lasting blood levels but still lasts hours.
source: Harris 2003 Drug Alcohol Depend; Mendelson 2006 Clin Pharmacol Ther; Kirkpatrick 2012 Psychopharmacology

why: Methamphetamine's half-life is ~10 h, so wakefulness and stimulation persist far longer than cocaine's.
source: Cook 1993 Drug Metab Dispos; Harris 2003; Cruickshank & Dyer 2009 Addiction

why: Intranasal cocaine euphoria starts within minutes, peaks at ~15-45 min and is largely gone in 1-2 h.
source: Javaid 1978 Science; Van Dyke 1978; Resnick 1977; Volkow 1997 Nature

why: Intranasal cocaine stimulation follows its short ~1 h half-life and fades within 1-2 h.
source: Javaid 1978 Science; Fischman 1983; Jeffcoat 1989 Drug Metab Dispos

why: Nicotine from a cigarette hits the brain in seconds; the 'head rush' and arousal peak within minutes and fade within about half an hour.
source: Benowitz 2009 Annu Rev Pharmacol Toxicol; Henningfield 1985; Perkins 1994 Psychopharmacology

why: Pleasant/'liking' ratings after a cigarette peak within minutes and drop off quickly as brain nicotine redistributes.
source: Henningfield 1985 J Pharmacol Exp Ther; Perkins 1994; Benowitz 2009

why: Alcohol's pleasant stimulation is strongest on the rising blood-alcohol limb (~30-60 min) and fades as levels fall.
source: Martin 1993 Alcohol Clin Exp Res (BAES); King 2002/2011 Arch Gen Psychiatry; Holdstock & de Wit 1998

why: Sedation from alcohol peaks later than stimulation, on the falling blood-alcohol limb 1-3 h after drinking.
source: Martin 1993 (BAES sedation subscale); King 2011 Arch Gen Psychiatry; Roehrs & Roth 2001

why: Two drinks reduce tension/anxiety for a couple of hours, tracking blood alcohol.
source: Sayette 1993 Psychol Bull; Donohue 2007; Curtin 2001 Psychol Sci

why: Oral diazepam is absorbed fast (Tmax ~1 h); sedation peaks at 1-2 h and fades over several hours as it redistributes, despite its long half-life.
source: Greenblatt 1980; Mattila 1988; Ellinwood 1985 Psychopharmacology

why: Anxiety relief from 5 mg diazepam begins within the first hour and lasts several hours.
source: Greenblatt & Shader 1974; Ashton 1994 Drugs; de Wit 1984

why: 100 mg MDMA effects begin at 30-60 min, peak at 1.5-2.5 h and end by 4-6 h.
source: Liechti 2001; Hysek 2014; Vizeli & Liechti 2017 J Psychopharmacol; Holze 2020 Neuropsychopharmacology

why: Feelings of closeness and trust ('empathogenic') follow the same 1.5-3 h peak and fade by about 5-6 h.
source: Hysek 2014 Soc Cogn Affect Neurosci; Kirkpatrick 2014; Holze 2020

why: MDMA stimulates (heart rate, energy) with a peak around 2 h, in step with its other acute effects.
source: Liechti 2001; Hysek 2011; Vizeli & Liechti 2017

why: After smoking, the cannabis 'high' starts within minutes, peaks at 15-45 min and is mostly gone after 2-3 h.
source: Huestis 1992 Pharmacol Biochem Behav; Hart 2001; Grotenhermen 2003 Clin Pharmacokinet; Hindocha 2015

why: Altered time and sensory perception after smoking follows the same fast rise and 2-3 h decline.
source: Huestis 1992; D'Souza 2004 Neuropsychopharmacology; Zuurman 2009 Br J Clin Pharmacol

why: Smoked cannabis increases appetite and food intake within the first hour or two ('munchies').
source: Foltin 1988 Appetite; Kirkham 2005; Hart 2002

why: Oral 10 mg morphine/oxycodone gives pain relief from ~30 min, peaking at 1-2 h and lasting about 4 h.
source: Hoskin 1989 Br J Clin Pharmacol; Lugo & Kern 2002; analgesic textbooks (Goodman & Gilman)

why: Respiratory depression from an oral opioid follows plasma levels with a slight delay, peaking 1-2 h after dosing.
source: Dahan 2010 Anesthesiology; Pattinson 2008 Br J Anaesth

why: Injected or smoked heroin gives a 'rush' within seconds to minutes; the high then settles and fades over a few hours.
source: Comer 1999 Psychopharmacology; Rook 2006 Clin Pharmacokinet; Mello 1980

why: Breathing suppression from heroin is fastest and deepest in the first 30 min, which is why overdoses happen soon after use.
source: Darke 2003 Addiction; Dahan 2010 Anesthesiology; White & Irvine 1999 Addiction

why: After the rush, users 'nod' (drowsy) for a few hours as heroin's morphine metabolite acts.
source: Comer 1999; Rook 2006; Jenkins 1994 J Anal Toxicol

why: Dissociation during a 40-min ketamine infusion peaks near the end of the infusion and resolves within about 1-2 h of starting.
source: Zarate 2006 Arch Gen Psychiatry; Murrough 2013 Am J Psychiatry; Luckenbaugh 2014 J Affect Disord

why: In depression, ketamine's antidepressant effect appears within hours, peaks around 1 day and fades over about 3-7 days.
source: Berman 2000 Biol Psychiatry; Zarate 2006 Arch Gen Psychiatry; Murrough 2013; Wilkinson 2018 meta-analysis

why: Sub-anaesthetic ketamine reduces pain during and shortly after infusion, fading within 1-2 h of stopping.
source: Olofsen 2012 Anesthesiology; Sigtermans 2009; Niesters 2014 Br J Clin Pharmacol

why: Psilocybin perceptual effects begin at 20-40 min, peak at 1.5-2.5 h and end by about 5-6 h.
source: Hasler 2004 Psychopharmacology; Griffiths 2011; Holze 2022 JAMA Psychiatry; Brown 2017 Clin Pharmacokinet

why: Positive mood/'good drug effect' follows the same arc as the overall psilocybin experience.
source: Griffiths 2006/2011 Psychopharmacology; Holze 2022 JAMA Psychiatry

why: 100 ug LSD effects start at 30-60 min, peak at 2-3 h and last about 8-10 h.
source: Dolder 2017 Clin Pharmacokinet; Holze 2019/2021 Neuropsychopharmacology; Schmid 2015 Biol Psychiatry

why: Positive mood and 'good drug effect' after LSD peak around 2-4 h and persist through most of the 8-10 h experience.
source: Schmid 2015 Biol Psychiatry; Dolder 2016; Holze 2021

why: Daytime melatonin 0.5-1 mg peaks in blood within ~1 h and causes mild drowsiness for a few hours (half-life ~45 min).
source: Dollins 1994 PNAS; Zhdanova 1995/2001; Harpsoe 2015 Eur J Clin Pharmacol

why: Mild loss of alertness tracks the short-lived melatonin peak.
source: Dollins 1994 PNAS; Lieberman 1984 Brain Res

why: Propranolol peaks in blood at 1-2 h and blocks the bodily signs of anxiety for roughly 6-12 h.
source: Shand 1975 N Engl J Med; Steenen 2016 J Psychopharmacol (meta-analysis); Brantigan 1982

why: Lower heart rate and mild calming after 40 mg follow its 1-3 h peak and several-hour duration.
source: Shand 1975; Turner 1976; Steenen 2016

why: IR guanfacine peaks in blood at 1-4 h with a ~17 h half-life, so drowsiness builds over hours and lasts most of the day.
source: Cornish 1988 Br J Clin Pharmacol; Kiechel 1986; Jerie 1980; Sorkin & Heel 1986 Drugs

why: Alpha-2A agonism lowers noradrenergic tone and alertness with the same slow, long time course.
source: Cornish 1988; Sorkin & Heel 1986 Drugs; Arnsten 2007

why: Oral haloperidol peaks at 2-6 h with a ~20 h half-life; sedation in healthy volunteers is delayed and long.
source: Froemming 1989 Clin Pharmacokinet; King 1995; Barbanoj 2001

why: Dopamine D2 blockade lowers drive and reward-seeking (dysphoria) with a slow onset and day-long duration.
source: Pessiglione 2006 Nature; Lane 1999; Kapur 2000 Am J Psychiatry

why: A single 50 mg dose can cause mild nausea/appetite loss that follows its slow peak (Tmax 4-8 h) and long half-life (~26 h).
source: DeVane 2002 Clin Pharmacokinet; Ronfeld 1997; product label

why: Bupropion mildly increases alertness after its plasma peak (2-3 h, SR formulation later), lasting much of the day.
source: Jefferson 2005 Prim Care Companion; Hamilton 1995; Rush 1998 Psychopharmacology

why: Phenelzine irreversibly blocks MAO, so a single 15 mg dose has small, slow and long-lasting activating effects; acute subjective data are sparse.
source: Robinson 1985; Kennedy 2000 J Clin Psychiatry; product label

why: At 25 mg CBD has at most small calming effects, peaking a few hours after oral oil (Tmax 1-4 h).
source: Millar 2018 Front Pharmacol; Zuardi 2017; Arndt & de Wit 2017 Cannabis Cannabinoid Res

why: 200 mg L-theanine peaks in blood at ~1 h and gives mild relaxation for a few hours.
source: Kimura 2007 Biol Psychol; Scheid 2012 Amino Acids; Hidese 2019 Nutrients

why: Semaglutide peaks 1-3 days after injection and has a ~1-week half-life, so appetite suppression from one dose lasts weeks.
source: Hall 2018 Clin Pharmacol Ther (pharmacokinetics); Blundell 2017 Diabetes Obes Metab; Friedrichsen 2021

why: Moderate-vigorous exercise improves mood during and for an hour or two after the session ('afterglow').
source: Reed & Ones 2006 Psychol Sport Exerc (meta-analysis); Ekkekakis 2011 Sports Med

why: Anxiety rises within minutes of an acute stressor and falls back soon after it ends.
source: Kirschbaum 1993 TSST; Dickerson & Kemeny 2004 Psychol Bull; Allen 2017 Neurosci Biobehav Rev

why: Feeling connected rises during warm time with friends and fades within an hour or two after parting.
source: Dunbar 2012 Proc R Soc B; Heinrichs 2003 Biol Psychiatry; Kok & Fredrickson 2010

why: Hunger falls during a meal, is lowest shortly after, and returns over the next 3-5 h.
source: Blundell 2010 Obes Rev (satiety methods); Cummings 2001 Diabetes (ghrelin); Flint 2000 Int J Obes
